answer: Demonstrating that a program improves outcomes is necessary but not sufficient for a policy decision, because every dollar spent on one program is a dollar not spent on another. Economists call the value of that forgone alternative the opportunity cost, and it reframes the question from 'Does it work?' to 'Is it worth it, given the alternatives?' In this CAPHE lab, an intensive program that produces more health benefit per person can be the wrong choice when a cheaper program reaches more people and yields greater total benefit from the same fixed budget. Effectiveness analysis tells what works; efficiency analysis tells what to do about it.

faqs.q: What is opportunity cost in program evaluation?
faqs.a: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up when money is committed to one program. The true cost of a program includes the health benefits forgone by not funding the alternative.

faqs.q: Why isn't 'it works' enough to justify funding a program?
faqs.a: Knowing a program improves outcomes says nothing about whether it is the best use of a limited budget. A more intensive program can be less efficient if a cheaper one reaches more people and produces greater total benefit per dollar.

faqs.q: How does a fixed budget change the comparison between programs?
faqs.a: Under a fixed budget, the relevant metric is health benefit per dollar, not benefit per person. The lab's simulator shows a cheaper program generating about 20% more total health benefit from the same $100,000 by reaching more participants.

faqs.q: How do efficiency and equity relate in this framework?
faqs.a: They can align. A program that reaches twice as many people at lower cost may also serve more underserved populations, so the more efficient option can advance equity as well as total health gain.
